Summary and Source: No reputable news or government statement found regarding Algeria's response to the USTR Section 301 forced labor investigation.

No reputable news or government statement found regarding Angola's response. Only generic coverage of Angola's inclusion in the tariff list (~$889M in exports, mostly petroleum) was found (360mozambique.com).

Argentina signed a U.S.-Argentina Agreement on Reciprocal Trade and Investment (ARTI) in Feb 2026 including a commitment to prohibit forced-labor imports, placing it in USTR's lower 10% tariff tier. No specific Argentine government statement/protest on the July hearings was found. Source: White & Case / Gibson Dunn (law firm summaries of USTR determination).
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No (committed via trade agreement, not yet implemented as domestic law per USTR)

Summary and Source: Trade Minister Don Farrell rejected USTR's finding, calling the tariffs "unjustified and inconsistent" with the US-Australia FTA and asserting Australia already has "world-leading" modern slavery legislation. Source: HCAMag, June 3, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No (Modern Slavery Act 2018 is a reporting regime, not an import prohibition)

Summary and Source: The Davis administration amended the Customs Management Act (new section 208A) via 2026-2027 Budget legislation to allow customs to prohibit forced/child-labor goods, targeting passage around July 1, 2026, partly to move from the 12.5% to 10% tariff tier. Source: The Tribune (Bahamas), June 25, 2026.
No reputable news or government statement found regarding Bahrain's response.

Under a Feb 2026 US-Bangladesh Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, Bangladesh committed to adopt a forced-labor import prohibition and strengthen labor-law enforcement, earning it the lower 10% tariff tier. No implementing domestic law found yet. Source: USTR Fact Sheet (US-Bangladesh ART) / Dhaka Tribune, June 3, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No (committed via trade agreement, not yet implemented as domestic law)

Summary and Source: Brazil's government called the tariff proposal "regrettable" and "absurd," citing its ILO-recognized record combating forced labor. Separately, Brazil's Chamber of Deputies fast-tracked a long-dormant forced-labor import ban bill (originally 2015, cocoa-focused, now expanded to all products) through committee. Source: WWD/Sourcing Journal, June 16, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No (bill advanced through committee but not yet enacted as of research date)

Summary and Source: Cambodia engaged in consultations with USTR and adopted Interministerial Regulation No. 450 MEF.PrK, "Prohibition on Imports of Goods Linked to Forced Labor," effective July 1, 2026, jointly run by the Ministries of Economy/Finance, Commerce, and Labour. This secured Cambodia the lower 10% tariff tier. Source: BowerGroupAsia, June 7, 2026; ielp.worldtradelaw.net, July 10, 2026.

Canada has had a forced-labor import prohibition since July 1, 2020 (Customs Tariff item 9897.00.00) but USTR flagged weak enforcement (only 2 shipments ever actually prohibited). In response, Canada tabled Bill C-35 on June 12, 2026 to strengthen the ban with a new supply-chain tracing framework, while disputing that additional US duties are warranted. Source: Global Affairs Canada (official), June 12, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (existing ban since 2020; being strengthened via Bill C-35)

Summary and Source: Chile's government said it is pursuing "constructive dialogue" rather than confrontation, meeting USTR Amb. Greer to seek exclusion from the 12.5% tariff; export associations lobbied in Washington ahead of the July 7 hearing. Source: Diario Financiero, June-July 2026.

China's Ministry of Commerce spokesperson said China "opposes all forms of unilateral restrictive measures," including those imposed "under the pretext of forced labor," and called for stable bilateral trade relations. Source: Global Times, early June 2026.

The Petro government submitted comments to USTR; domestic business groups (AmCham Colombia) publicly pressed the government to issue a decree explicitly banning forced-labor imports, but no such decree has been confirmed issued. Source: Infobae Colombia, June 25, 2026.

Foreign Trade Minister Indiana Trejos submitted formal comments to USTR (July 6) and testified at the July 7 hearing, arguing no evidence links Costa Rican exports to forced labor and requesting the tariff not be applied. Source: La Nación, July 7-8, 2026.
Industry Minister Eduardo Sanz Lovatón emphasized continued bilateral dialogue; labor union leader Pepe Abreu rejected the forced-labor accusation as inaccurate. Source: Diario Libre, June 3-9, 2026.

Ecuador's Vice Minister of Production said the March 2026 Reciprocal Trade Agreement with the US remains open for negotiation. Ecuador's COMEX Resolution 005-2026 (April 29, 2026) created an Inter-institutional Technical Team to restrict forced-labor-goods imports, though USTR found no enforcement actions had yet occurred. Source: Primicias, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (per USTR determination — ban exists, enforcement weak)

Summary and Source: No reputable source found for a specific Egyptian government reaction to this investigation.

El Salvador's customs authority issued decree DGA-032-2026 (published March 6, 2026, effective June 1, 2026) requiring sworn no-forced-labor declarations from importers. Separately, El Salvador's Reciprocal Trade Agreement with the US was confirmed (July 9) not yet in force, so El Salvador is still paying the 10% tariff. Source: La Prensa Gráfica, July 9, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (domestic customs decree in force since June 1, 2026, independent of the ART)

Summary and Source: The European Commission called the tariff threat "unjustified," stating its Forced Labour Regulation (EU) 2024/3015 is "one of the most ambitious instruments of its kind." USTR nonetheless found enforcement inadequate since the regulation isn't fully enforceable until Dec 2027. Source: Euronews, June 3, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (EU Forced Labour Regulation 2024/3015, in force but not yet fully enforceable until Dec 2027)

Summary and Source: Guatemala published a Ministerial Agreement in its Official Gazette (July 6, 2026) formally banning imports of forced-labor-made goods, fulfilling a commitment from its Jan 2026 Reciprocal Trade Agreement with the US. Guatemala also testified at the July 7 hearing. Source: Infobae Guatemala / Diario de Centro América, July 6, 2026.

Guyana's Ministry of Labour and Manpower Planning requested to appear at the USTR hearing to defend its record on blocking forced-labor-made imports. Source: Demerara Waves Online News, June 24, 2026.
A Honduran vice minister called the USTR probe an "opportunity for improvement" for labor inspection systems and said Honduras does not consider itself sanctioned. Source: Infobae, June 4, 2026.
No reputable source found reporting a Hong Kong government response; only general business-impact coverage (HKTDC Research, DHL) exists.

India's Commerce Ministry, APEDA, CII and FICCI pushed back on USTR's findings as unsupported. Separately, India's Directorate General of Foreign Trade issued a notification (~July 13-14, 2026) prohibiting import of goods made "wholly or in part" with forced labor — India's first such measure, issued just before this report. Source: Bloomberg, July 9, 2026; Business Standard, July 14, 2026.

Indonesia was credited by USTR with having a forced-labor import prohibition (Trade Regulation No. 9 of 2026, effective April 15, 2026) but enforcement was found weak; advocacy groups say "operational details are still missing." Source: Walk Free, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (per USTR determination — ban exists, enforcement weak)

Summary and Source: No reputable source found reporting an Iraqi government response.
No reputable source found reporting an Israeli government response; only business-impact coverage (Jerusalem Post) exists.

Japan submitted a written comment citing its July 2025 bilateral trade agreement with the US and asking for "appropriate actions" (implicit request for tariff relief). Source: International Economic Law and Policy Blog, July 2026.

Jordan requested to appear at USTR's July hearings to contest its 12.5% tariff placement. Separately (unrelated to Jordan's government response), CBP issued Withhold Release Orders in June 2026 against two Jordanian garment manufacturers. Source: International Economic Law and Policy Blog, July 2026.
Kazakhstan submitted written comments and requested to appear at USTR's July hearings to contest its 12.5% tariff placement. Source: International Economic Law and Policy Blog, July 2026.
No reputable source found regarding Kuwait's response to this specific investigation.
No reputable source found regarding Libya's response.

Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Johari Abdul Ghani told Parliament (June 23, 2026) that Malaysia is developing a mechanism to bar forced-labor-made imports via a new Inter-Agency Task Force on Forced Labour, citing US pressure directly. Source: The Edge Malaysia, June 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No (mechanism in development, not yet enacted; lower 10% tariff tier via ART commitment)

Summary and Source: Mexico's Undersecretary of Economy testified (July 7 hearing) that the proposed tariffs are "unjustified," arguing Mexico already has adequate enforcement. USTR still found Mexico's USMCA-linked ban weakly enforced. Source: Mexico Business News, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (per USTR determination — ban exists, enforcement weak)

Summary and Source: Morocco participated in confidential consultations with USTR, but "the consultations did not alter the outcome"; Morocco was found to lack a qualifying import ban. Source: Morocco World News, June 2026.
New Zealand's MFAT said the Trade Minister "made it clear that New Zealand disagrees with the findings" and would continue to register its disagreement with Washington. Source: MFAT (official), 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No (forced labor illegal domestically, but no import ban; a Modern Slavery Bill is in progress)

Summary and Source: No reputable source found regarding Nicaragua's response to this specific forced-labor investigation (note: Nicaragua is separately subject to an unrelated Section 301 action on labor/human rights from Dec 2025).

Nigeria submitted written comments to the USTR docket ahead of the July 7 hearings, per trade-law roundup coverage; specific content not detailed in available sources. Source: International Economic Law and Policy Blog, July 2026.

Norway submitted formal comments arguing the investigation unfairly groups it with countries with weaker regimes, citing its Transparency Act and forthcoming incorporation of the EU forced-labor regulation into the EEA Agreement. Source: Government of Norway (regjeringen.no), 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No (Transparency Act covers domestic due diligence, not an import prohibition)

Summary and Source: No reputable source found regarding Oman's response.
In late April 2026, Pakistan amended its Import Policy Order 2022 to explicitly bar forced-labor-made imports, reported as a move to avoid higher US tariffs. Source: Pakistan Today, April 30, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (per USTR determination and Pakistan's own April 2026 amendment — ban exists, enforcement weak)

Summary and Source: Peru's Director of Trade Negotiations testified at the July hearings seeking full exemption, citing over 216,000 domestic forced/child-labor enforcement actions in 2024; Peru indicated (April 2026) it was drafting but had not passed import-ban legislation. Source: Mining Weekly, July 8, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No (legislation reportedly in drafting, not enacted)

Summary and Source: DTI Undersecretary Allan Gepty submitted formal comments (July 6) seeking exemption, saying the Philippines is drafting a joint administrative order to formalize a forced-labor import investigation mechanism. Source: Philippine Daily Inquirer, July 6-7, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No (administrative order reportedly in drafting, not enacted)

Summary and Source: No reputable source found regarding Qatar's response. Qatar's 2026 domestic kafala/labor-law amendments concern worker protections, not an import ban.
No reputable source found regarding Russia's response to this specific investigation.
No reputable source found regarding Saudi Arabia's response. Existing kafala-system reforms concern domestic worker protections, not an import ban.

Singapore's Ministry of Trade and Industry said it will continue engaging USTR, calling forced labor "a transnational issue," and estimated a third of its US-bound exports could be affected. Source: The Online Citizen, June 4-5, 2026.

A South African government delegation (led by the dtic) testified at the July 9 hearing, citing ILO convention ratification and requesting exemption or category-specific carve-outs. Source: South African Department of Trade, Industry and Competition (official), July 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No (relies on ILO ratification, not a specific import-ban law)

Summary and Source: Korean officials told USTR the proposed 12.5% tariff is "neither appropriate nor necessary," citing a separate trade/investment agreement with the US; USTR reportedly asked Korea for a forced-labor enforcement plan. Source: The Korea Herald, ~July 10, 2026.

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake issued an order (effective July 10, 2026) banning imports of forced-labor-made goods and requiring importer certification, explicitly to protect ~$3B in apparel exports from the threatened tariff. Source: Newswire.lk, July 14, 2026.

The Swiss Federal Council rejected USTR's findings, saying Switzerland already prohibits forced labor under constitutional/civil/criminal law; SECO is separately negotiating a broader tariff settlement with Washington. Source: swissinfo.ch, June 3, 2026; Swiss government (admin.ch), June 5, 2026.

Taiwan was placed in the 10% tariff tier due to a commitment (Feb 2026 Reciprocal Trade Agreement) to ban forced-labor goods; Taiwan's government said it may dispute the proposal within the post-hearing window. Source: Focus Taiwan, June 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No (committed via trade agreement, not yet implemented as domestic law)

Summary and Source: Thailand's Cabinet (June 23, 2026) approved a new committee to set standards for forced-labor-risk imports, which will propose watchlist/blacklist designations under existing trade law; Thailand held technical talks with USTR in May. Source: Asia News Network / Mahanakorn Partners Group, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No (regulatory framework being built, not yet an enacted ban)

Summary and Source: No reputable source found regarding Trinidad and Tobago's response.
No reputable source found regarding Türkiye's response.
No reputable source found regarding the UAE's response.

USTR credited the UK with a "partial regime" (2023 Procurement Act forced-labor exclusions, 2025 Great British Energy Act provisions), securing the lower 10% tier. UK Trade Minister Chris Bryant said he'd be "amazed and demoralised" if the UK didn't pass "some form of forced labor ban" before ~2029. Source: WWD/Sourcing Journal, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (procurement exclusions + Modern Slavery Act reporting; no full import prohibition)

Summary and Source: Uruguay's Ministry of Economy and Finance rejected USTR's characterization and sent officials to Washington for technical consultations on its import-control procedures. Source: La Mañana (Uruguay), 2026.
No country-specific government response found; context complicated by reported US intervention/change in Venezuelan leadership in Jan 2026, predating USTR's June determination.

Vietnam's Foreign Ministry rejected USTR's findings as not accurately reflecting "Vietnam's efforts in preventing, mitigating, and reducing forced labor," and pledged continued engagement with the US. Source: The Diplomat / Vietnam News Agency, June 4, 2026.
